triage.name: Rotator Cuff Injuries
triage.reason: Very common shoulder complaint with a clear diagnosis reachable by history, provocative maneuvers and imaging; mimics include adhesive capsulitis and impingement.

presentation: older format without SNOMED terms
exam: older format without SNOMED terms

demographics: More common with increasing age; most cases are degenerative wear-and-tear in adults over 40
Athletes in overhead sports (baseball pitching, swimming, tennis) and manual workers who reach overhead or lift heavily are affected at younger ages
Traumatic full-thickness tears are more common in men; degenerative tears are more evenly distributed

risk_factors.text: Age over 40 with cumulative shoulder use
Repetitive overhead activity (throwing, swimming, painting, carpentry, stocking shelves)
Heavy lifting or repetitive shoulder loading at work
Acute fall onto an outstretched arm or sudden heavy lift
Shoulder impingement or prior shoulder injury

social_history: Occupations or hobbies requiring repeated overhead reaching or heavy lifting
Participation in overhead or throwing sports

chief_complaints.text: My shoulder hurts, especially when I lift my arm
I can't reach behind my back or overhead like I used to
My arm feels weak when I try to lift things
It hurts at night when I lie on that side

hpi.onset: Gradual over weeks to months with no clear injury in degenerative cases; sudden after a fall, a pull, or lifting a heavy object in acute tears
hpi.duration: Weeks to months for degenerative tendinopathy or bursitis; hours to days for an acute traumatic tear
hpi.progression: Slowly worsening with continued activity; pain may plateau or improve with rest, while weakness and loss of motion tend to persist or progress
hpi.location: Top and outer part of the shoulder and upper arm, over the deltoid and lateral shoulder
hpi.radiation: May spread down the outer upper arm toward the elbow; does not go past the elbow
hpi.quality: Dull, aching or sore at rest; sharp and catching with overhead or reaching movements
hpi.severity: Mild to moderate at rest, moderate to severe with activity; often 4–7/10 with movement
hpi.timing: Worse with activity and at night; may wake the patient when rolling onto the affected side
aggravating: Lifting the arm overhead or to the side
Reaching behind the back (e.g., fastening a bra, reaching a back pocket)
Pulling or pushing with the arm
Carrying or lifting objects away from the body
relieving: Keeping the arm at the side
Ice or heat to the shoulder
Sleeping propped up or on the other side

associated_symptoms.text: Weakness lifting the arm or carrying objects
Clicking, catching or popping with shoulder movement
Stiffness or difficulty with overhead reach
Pain referred down the outer arm

pertinent_negatives: Numbness, tingling or electric shocks down the arm or into the hand
Neck pain radiating into the arm
Severe pain and deformity after a fall (suggests dislocation or fracture)
Inability to move the shoulder at all in any direction
Fever, redness, warmth or swelling of the joint
Unexplained weight loss or night sweats

positives.text: Night pain when lying on the shoulder
Clicking or catching in the shoulder

negatives: Locking or giving way of the shoulder
Numbness or tingling in the arm or hand
Weakness in the hand or grip
Neck pain radiating into the arm
Redness or warmth over the shoulder

atypical.how_it_differs: Degenerative full-thickness tears are very common and may cause little or no pain; patients often present with weakness, difficulty lifting the arm, or a painless loss of overhead reach rather than severe pain.

Rotator cuff tears are rare in children; shoulder pain in this age group is more often from overuse apophysitis, Little League shoulder, or instability, and the history usually centers on throwing or overhead sport.
Tendon healing is impaired and symptoms may be more persistent; frozen shoulder (adhesive capsulitis) is more common and can mask or accompany a cuff problem with prominent stiffness.

general.mild: Comfortable at rest, holds the arm at the side, moves the shoulder without obvious distress
general.moderate: Guards the affected arm, winces when lifting the arm overhead or reaching behind the back
general.severe: Holds the arm protectively against the body, avoids active shoulder movement, distressed with passive motion
general.critical: Not applicable to this condition; a toxic or systemically unwell appearance should prompt evaluation for another cause

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to actively abduct the arm slowly from the side to overhead while watching for the point of pain
findings.finding: Pain in the mid-range of abduction (roughly 60–120 degrees) that eases as the arm approaches overhead

findings.maneuver: Test resisted abduction with the arm at the side or in the scapular plane (empty can / Jobe test)
findings.finding: Weakness and pain with resisted abduction, worse than the opposite side

findings.maneuver: Test resisted external rotation with the elbow at the side
findings.finding: Weakness with resisted external rotation, suggesting infraspinatus or teres minor involvement

findings.maneuver: Passively abduct the arm to 90 degrees and ask the patient to lower it slowly
findings.finding: The arm drops suddenly or the patient cannot lower it smoothly, indicating a large or full-thickness tear

findings.maneuver: Stabilize the scapula and passively flex the arm forward overhead (Neer impingement sign)
findings.finding: Pain reproduced in the shoulder with forward flexion

findings.maneuver: Flex the shoulder to 90 degrees, flex the elbow, and internally rotate the arm (Hawkins–Kennedy test)
findings.finding: Pain reproduced in the shoulder with internal rotation

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to place the hand behind the back and lift it away from the lumbar spine (lift-off / Gerber test)
findings.finding: Inability to lift the hand off the back or marked weakness, suggesting subscapularis involvement

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to lie on the affected side or press the shoulder into the examining table
findings.finding: Reproduction of the characteristic night pain

findings.maneuver: Passively move the shoulder through flexion, abduction, and rotation
findings.finding: Passive range of motion is preserved or near-normal (unlike adhesive capsulitis, where passive motion is also restricted)

findings.maneuver: Palpate the cervical paraspinals and perform Spurling maneuver
findings.finding: No neck tenderness and no reproduction of arm pain with neck extension and rotation

findings.maneuver: Test sensation, grip strength, and radial pulse in the affected arm
findings.finding: Intact sensation, normal grip strength, and palpable distal pulses

findings.maneuver: Inspect and palpate the shoulder joint for swelling, warmth, or erythema
findings.finding: No joint effusion, warmth, or erythema

findings.maneuver: Inspect the shoulder contour and compare with the opposite side
findings.finding: No obvious deformity or squaring of the shoulder (which would suggest dislocation or fracture)

imaging.study: Shoulder x-ray (anteroposterior and scapular Y or axillary views)
imaging.preferred_when: First-line imaging for any shoulder pain; rules out fracture, dislocation, and arthritis

findings.text: Normal bony alignment and joint spaces; no fracture or dislocation
Acromiohumeral interval narrowed to less than 7 mm, suggesting a chronic large or full-thickness tear
Superior migration of the humeral head

imaging.study: MRI of the shoulder without contrast
imaging.preferred_when: Suspected full-thickness tear, failed conservative care, or preoperative planning

findings.text: Tendon thickening, increased intrasubstance signal, or partial-thickness tear of the supraspinatus
Full-thickness tendon defect with fluid signal extending through the tendon
Tendon retraction and muscle atrophy or fatty infiltration in chronic tears
Subacromial-subdeltoid bursitis with fluid in the bursa

imaging.preferred_when: Office-based evaluation of a suspected tear; avoids radiation and is cheaper than MRI

findings.text: Hypoechoic or anechoic tendon defect consistent with a partial- or full-thickness tear
Tendon thinning, heterogeneity, or calcification suggesting tendinopathy
Dynamic impingement of the tendon under the acromion with abduction

imaging.preferred_when: Suspected partial-thickness articular-sided tear or labral injury when standard MRI is equivocal

findings.text: Contrast extending into the articular surface of the tendon, confirming a partial-thickness tear

initial.test: Shoulder x-ray (anteroposterior and scapular Y or axillary views)
initial.why: First-line imaging to exclude fracture, dislocation, and glenohumeral arthritis and to look for chronic tear signs
Office-based, low-cost test that can confirm a full-thickness tear
initial.only_if: a full-thickness tear is suspected and MRI is not immediately available

confirmatory.test: MRI of the shoulder without contrast
confirmatory.why: Most accurate noninvasive test for tear size, retraction, and muscle quality; guides surgery

supporting.why: Detects partial-thickness articular-sided tears and labral injury
supporting.only_if: standard MRI is equivocal and surgery is being considered

not_indicated.why: No role in a mechanical shoulder problem unless infection or systemic illness is suspected
Not needed for routine rotator cuff injury; reserved for suspected infection or inflammatory arthritis
Not needed for routine rotator cuff injury; reserved for suspected infection or inflammatory arthritis

decision_points: Order shoulder x-ray first in any acute shoulder injury to exclude fracture or dislocation before attributing pain to the cuff
Choose ultrasound when a tear is suspected and MRI is unavailable or contraindicated; choose MRI when surgery is being considered or the tear extent must be defined
Do not image a mild, atraumatic shoulder pain that improves with conservative care unless symptoms persist beyond 6 to 12 weeks
Consider adhesive capsulitis when passive range of motion is also restricted, and cervical radiculopathy when neck pain or neurologic symptoms are present

differential.name: Adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder)
differential.why_considered: Shoulder pain with progressive loss of motion, worse at night, in the same middle-aged population

history: Gradual onset with progressive global stiffness rather than activity-related pain
Difficulty with both active and passive movement in all directions
More common in diabetes and after immobilization
exam: Passive range of motion is also markedly restricted, especially external rotation
Global loss of motion rather than weakness in a specific tendon
imaging: Normal rotator cuff on MRI or ultrasound
Thickened coracohumeral ligament and axillary recess on MRI

differential.name: Subacromial impingement syndrome
differential.why_considered: Overhead shoulder pain with a painful arc, very common in the same repetitive-use population

history: Pain with overhead activity but no significant weakness or night pain
Symptoms improve with activity modification and therapy
exam: Strength is preserved; no drop-arm sign
imaging: No tendon defect on ultrasound or MRI
Subacromial bursal fluid or acromial spur may be present

differential.name: Cervical radiculopathy
differential.why_considered: Shoulder and arm pain that can mimic a cuff problem, especially with radiation down the arm
differential.trigger: Neck pain or numbness, tingling, or weakness in a dermatomal pattern

history: Neck pain radiating into the arm in a dermatomal distribution
Numbness, tingling, or electric shocks in the hand
Pain worsened by neck extension or rotation
exam: Positive Spurling maneuver reproduces arm pain
Dermatomal sensory loss, diminished reflex, or myotomal weakness
imaging: Cervical spine MRI showing nerve root compression
Normal rotator cuff on shoulder imaging

differential.name: Glenohumeral osteoarthritis
differential.why_considered: Chronic shoulder pain and stiffness in older adults

history: Deep, aching pain with progressive stiffness over years
Pain with all movements, not just overhead
imaging: Joint space narrowing, osteophytes, and subchondral sclerosis on x-ray

differential.name: Acromioclavicular joint arthritis
differential.why_considered: Top-of-shoulder pain that can be confused with cuff pain

history: Pain localized to the top of the shoulder, worse with cross-body reaching
History of prior AC joint injury
exam: Tenderness directly over the AC joint
imaging: AC joint space narrowing and osteophytes on x-ray

differential.name: Acute shoulder dislocation
differential.why_considered: Sudden shoulder pain and weakness after trauma
differential.trigger: Obvious deformity, severe pain, or inability to move the shoulder after a fall

history: Sudden severe pain after a fall or injury
Inability to move the shoulder at all
exam: Squaring of the shoulder or palpable humeral head anteriorly
Marked restriction of all active and passive motion
imaging: Humeral head displaced from the glenoid on x-ray

differential.name: Proximal humerus fracture
differential.why_considered: Acute shoulder pain and weakness after a fall, especially in older adults
differential.trigger: Severe pain, swelling, ecchymosis, or deformity after a fall

history: Acute severe pain immediately after a fall
exam: Swelling, ecchymosis, and focal tenderness over the proximal humerus
imaging: Fracture line visible on shoulder x-ray

differential.name: Septic arthritis of the shoulder
differential.why_considered: Shoulder pain with systemic symptoms, though rare
differential.trigger: Fever, chills, or a hot swollen joint

imaging: Joint effusion on ultrasound or MRI

severity.mild: Tendinopathy or bursitis with mild pain only with overhead activity, no weakness, full active range of motion, and no night pain
severity.moderate: Persistent pain with activity and at night, painful arc, mild weakness with resisted testing, and difficulty with overhead reach but no drop-arm sign
severity.severe: Large or full-thickness tear with marked weakness, positive drop-arm sign, significant night pain, and inability to lift the arm overhead or reach behind the back

red_flags.finding: Inability to move the shoulder in any direction after trauma
red_flags.meaning: Possible dislocation or fracture; obtain x-ray before attributing to the cuff

red_flags.finding: Obvious deformity or squaring of the shoulder
Fever, chills, or a hot swollen joint
red_flags.meaning: Septic arthritis; needs urgent aspiration and antibiotics

red_flags.finding: Numbness, tingling, or weakness in a dermatomal pattern
red_flags.meaning: Cervical radiculopathy or nerve injury, not a simple cuff problem

red_flags.finding: Unexplained weight loss, night sweats, or history of cancer

complications.name: Chronic shoulder stiffness or adhesive capsulitis
clues: Global loss of passive range of motion

complications.name: Rotator cuff arthropathy
clues: Chronic large tear with superior humeral head migration

complications.name: Postoperative infection or stiffness after repair
clues: Fever, wound drainage, or increasing pain after surgery

special_populations.differences: Degenerative full-thickness tears are very common and may cause little or no pain; patients often present with weakness or painless loss of overhead reach rather than severe pain.
Rotator cuff tears are rare; shoulder pain is more often from overuse apophysitis, Little League shoulder, or instability, and the history usually centers on throwing or overhead sport.
Tendon healing is impaired and symptoms may be more persistent; frozen shoulder is more common and can mask or accompany a cuff problem with prominent stiffness.

key_questions.question: When did the shoulder pain start, and was there an injury or a specific event?
key_questions.looking_for: Gradual onset over weeks to months suggests degenerative tendinopathy or bursitis; sudden onset after a fall onto an outstretched arm or a heavy lift suggests an acute tear

key_questions.question: Where exactly is the pain, and does it spread anywhere?
key_questions.looking_for: Top and outer shoulder and upper arm, radiating down the outer arm but not past the elbow; pain past the elbow or into the hand suggests a neck or nerve problem

key_questions.question: What movements bring the pain on?
key_questions.looking_for: Overhead reaching, lifting the arm to the side or front, and reaching behind the back (fastening a bra, back pocket); this is the classic activity-related pattern

key_questions.question: Does it hurt at night, or when you lie on that shoulder?
key_questions.looking_for: Night pain that wakes the patient or pain when rolling onto the affected side supports a rotator cuff problem

key_questions.question: Have you noticed weakness in the arm, or does it feel like it might give way?
key_questions.looking_for: Weakness lifting the arm or carrying objects suggests a tear rather than simple tendinitis or bursitis

key_questions.question: Do you hear or feel clicking, catching, or popping when you move the shoulder?
key_questions.looking_for: Clicking or catching with movement is sometimes reported with cuff tears

key_questions.question: Do you have numbness, tingling, or electric shocks in the arm or hand?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent in a simple cuff problem; present symptoms point to cervical radiculopathy or a nerve injury

key_questions.question: Do you have neck pain that shoots into the arm?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; neck pain radiating into the arm suggests cervical radiculopathy instead

key_questions.question: What do you do for work or sport — any repeated overhead reaching or heavy lifting?
key_questions.looking_for: Occupations like carpentry, construction, or painting, and overhead sports such as swimming, tennis, or baseball pitching, raise the likelihood of a cuff injury

key_questions.question: Have you had a shoulder injury, shoulder surgery, or been told you have impingement or bursitis before?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior shoulder injury or impingement supports a cuff problem; prior surgery changes the workup

key_questions.question: Do you have diabetes or any other long-term medical conditions?
key_questions.looking_for: Diabetes is associated with more persistent tendon symptoms and a higher chance of frozen shoulder

key_questions.question: Have you taken any antibiotics in the last few months, especially for an infection?
key_questions.looking_for: Fluoroquinolone use is a risk factor for tendon injury

key_questions.question: Have you had a fever, chills, or unintentional weight loss?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; fever or a hot swollen joint suggests septic arthritis, and weight loss or night sweats raises concern for malignancy

key_questions.question: After any injury, could you move the shoulder at all, and is there any deformity?
key_questions.looking_for: Inability to move the shoulder in any direction or an obvious deformity suggests dislocation or fracture and needs x-ray first

reasoning_points: Middle-aged or older adult with shoulder pain worsened by overhead reaching and reaching behind the back
Pain localized to the top and outer shoulder and upper arm, not radiating past the elbow
Night pain when lying on the affected shoulder
Weakness with lifting or reaching, suggesting tendon involvement rather than simple bursitis
Painful arc of abduction and weakness with resisted abduction or external rotation on exam
Passive range of motion preserved, which argues against adhesive capsulitis
No neck pain, numbness, or tingling, which argues against cervical radiculopathy
Shoulder x-ray excludes fracture and dislocation; ultrasound or MRI confirms a tendon tear when surgery is considered

easy: Adult over 40 with gradual shoulder pain worse with overhead activity
Night pain when lying on the affected side
Painful arc of abduction and weakness with resisted abduction
No history of trauma, no neurologic symptoms
medium: Acute onset after a fall onto an outstretched arm with new weakness
Older adult with painless loss of overhead reach and no clear injury
Patient with diabetes and prominent stiffness that raises concern for frozen shoulder
Overhead athlete with shoulder pain and clicking
hard: Older adult with minimal pain but marked weakness and a drop-arm sign
Patient with neck pain and arm tingling that mimics cervical radiculopathy
Shoulder pain after trauma with inability to move the arm, requiring fracture or dislocation to be excluded first
Chronic large tear with superior humeral head migration and features of rotator cuff arthropathy
